transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me. I hope I'm not taking up too much of your time. 

Um... well, my lieutenant at the station—I'm an EMT—he's actually the one who sent me here. I think it was mostly just a misunderstanding, really. I was just trying to make sure things were set up right, so I kept moving the airway bags into this specific pattern. I just knew it was the right way they needed to be, you know? And I guess I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud while I did it. It wasn't meant to be disruptive or anything, I promise. 

But when my lieutenant told me to stop and step away... I wouldn't do it. I'm usually really good at following orders, I swear I'm a good worker, but I just couldn't stop. It just felt like the whole ambulance bay would go bad if I broke the sequence right then. I really didn't mean to cause a problem for anyone. Does... does that make sense to you?

When you were arranging those airway bags in that specific pattern, did you feel like you were trying to stop an unwanted thought or worry from happening, or did it just feel like the bags simply had to be in that exact order because it was the right way?

Um... well, it wasn't really a worry, exactly. I wasn't trying to stop a bad thought or anything like that. I know how that sounds, like maybe I was just being obsessive, but I promise it wasn't like that. 

It just... it just felt like they had to be that way. Like the pattern was already there, and I just needed to make the bags match it. It was just the right way for them to be, you know? I really didn't mean to make a big deal out of it. I'm usually very flexible with how we stock the rig. I hope you don't think I'm the kind of guy who just ignores his lieutenant. I really do try to be a good team player. Does that answer your question okay?

Before you felt the need to arrange those bags in that specific pattern, did you have any unwanted thoughts or worries running through your mind—even if they seemed silly—that made you feel like you had to do the arranging?

No, no, nothing like that. I didn't have any bad thoughts or worries beforehand. I know sometimes people do things like that because they're stressed or anxious, but I was feeling totally fine, honestly. 

I just... I just saw how they needed to be, and I did it. I wasn't trying to fix a bad thought or anything. I really hope I'm explaining this right. I don't want you to think I'm making things up or hiding anything from you. I just didn't have any weird thoughts before I moved the bags. Is that what you were asking?

Looking back on it now, do you think arranging those bags in that specific pattern was reasonable and necessary, or do you recognize it might have been excessive or more important than it needed to be?

Um... well, looking back now, I guess... I mean, I can see how it might have looked a little, you know, excessive to my lieutenant. I really do respect him, and I definitely don't want to seem like I'm making excuses. 

But at the time, it really just felt necessary. Like, it wasn't about me wanting to cause trouble or make a big production out of it. It just felt like the absolute right thing to do in that moment. I know it probably sounds a little strange now, sitting here talking about it, but it didn't feel unreasonable then. I just wanted to make sure things were set up the way they were supposed to be. 

I really hope that doesn't make me sound difficult to work with. I'm usually very easygoing, I promise. Do you think it's normal to sometimes just feel like things have to be a certain way, even if it looks a little odd to other people?

When you think about arranging things in a specific way or following certain patterns, does it ever feel like these thoughts or urges are coming from outside of yourself—like they're not really 'you'—or does it feel like a natural part of how you are as a person?

Um... no, they definitely feel like they're coming from me. It's just me, just how I am. I don't hear voices telling me to do it or anything scary like that, I promise. I know that's something you guys have to check for, but it's really just my own thoughts. 

It just feels like a natural part of me wanting to do a good job and make sure everything is right on the rig. I really pride myself on being thorough. I don't want you to think I'm losing my mind or being controlled by something weird. It's just my own brain wanting things neat. Does that make sense? I hope I'm answering that the way you need me to.

When you're not at work, do you find yourself arranging or organizing things in specific ways in other parts of your life—like at home or in your personal time—or is this pattern mostly something that happens at the station?

Um, no, not really. I mean... I keep my apartment tidy, of course, because I think it's important to be responsible and have a clean living space. But I don't, like, line things up perfectly or spend hours organizing my pantry or anything like that. 

It's really just at work. You know, when you're an EMT, people's lives are on the line, so you just want to make absolutely sure the equipment is ready to go. So that's why I did it there. But at home, I'm pretty relaxed. I can just leave a book on the table and it doesn't bother me at all. 

I really try to leave work at work, you know? I hope that's a good thing. It's normal to be a little more particular at a job like mine, right? I'm not doing anything strange at home, I promise.
When you were arranging those bags at work, did it cause you any distress or anxiety if you couldn't complete it exactly the way you felt it needed to be done?

Um... no, not really. I mean, if the tones dropped for a call, I would just drop what I was doing and go right away. It wasn't like... I wasn't going to have a panic attack or get all upset if I couldn't finish it right that second. 

I really don't want you to think I'm, like, obsessing over it to the point where it gets in the way of my job. Patient care always comes first for me, absolutely. If my lieutenant or anyone else needed me to stop, I'd just stop. It was really just a preference to have it set up that way, not a... not something that made me feel anxious or distressed if I couldn't do it. 

I hope that shows I can be flexible? I really try to be easy to work with, and I'd never let a preference like that cause a problem on a shift. That's a good sign, right?
Has this feeling that things need to be arranged in a specific way been happening for a while now, or was this arrangement of the bags something new that just started recently?

Um... well, the thing with the bags, and... I guess the other stuff at the station that got everyone so worked up, like with the paperwork and the cameras... that's been going on for maybe about two months? 

It really hasn't been that long, I promise. It's just a recent thing, just me trying to make sure everything is secure and done right. I know my captain said people were getting alarmed, but I really didn't mean to make anyone uncomfortable. I was just trying to be thorough, you know? Two months isn't that long in the grand scheme of things, right? I'm sure it's just a phase and I can stop doing it if it's bothering people. I really want to make sure I'm doing what I'm supposed to be doing.

When you're arranging things at work or checking on the paperwork and cameras, do you ever have thoughts that something bad might happen if you don't do it exactly right—like someone could get hurt, or something could go wrong?

Um... well... I guess I should just be completely honest with you. I'm sorry, I know I told you a few minutes ago that I would just stop if someone asked me to, and I really, really want you to know that I'm usually a very good, obedient employee. I hope you aren't upset with me for not saying this right away... I was just so embarrassed. 

The truth is, the reason they actually sent me here is because... well, at the station, I kept moving the airway bags into a pattern that I just knew was right. And I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud while I was doing it. And... when my lieutenant told me to stop, I... I wouldn't step away. 

I swear I wasn't trying to be insubordinate or difficult! It's exactly like you just asked—in that moment, it felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. I felt like I absolutely had to finish it or everything would be ruined. 

I feel so ashamed that I didn't listen to my lieutenant. You can understand why I didn't want to admit that part at first, right? I really want to be seen as a good medic, and I know how bad that makes me look. I promise I'm usually very cooperative.

When you think back to those two months at the station, before you felt the need to arrange the bags or check the paperwork and cameras, did you ever have thoughts pop into your head that you couldn't get rid of—thoughts that something bad would happen or that things weren't safe—even if you tried to ignore them?

Um... no, not really. I mean, before all of this started happening a couple of months ago, I was just... normal, you know? Just doing my job, doing my best. I didn't have any thoughts like that stuck in my head or anything. I wasn't worried about things being unsafe or bad things happening out of nowhere. 

I've always just been really focused on patient care and being a solid part of the crew. I really hope you can see that this recent stuff isn't who I usually am. I've always been a really steady medic before all this. I'm telling you the truth about that, I promise. That makes sense, right? That this is just a weird, temporary thing and not how I usually am?

When you first started feeling like you had to arrange those bags in a specific pattern two months ago, did you have any thoughts going through your mind—even fleeting ones—that something bad would happen to the station or to people if you didn't do it exactly right, or did the urge to arrange them just come out of nowhere without any thought behind it?

Um... well, it wasn't like... I didn't have any specific thoughts about bad things happening, no. I really didn't. It's just... I just felt this urge, you know? Like I just *had* to do it. It wasn't because I thought the station would blow up or someone would die or anything terrible like that. I promise I'm not crazy like that. 

It was just... an urge. Like an itch you have to scratch. I didn't really think about it, I just felt compelled to make it look right. I know that probably sounds strange, and I'm really sorry if it doesn't make sense, but I'm trying to be as helpful as I can. Does that answer your question? I hope I'm explaining it okay. I really don't want you to think I was imagining all sorts of horrible disasters.

When you get the urge to arrange things or check on the paperwork and cameras, does it feel like your own thought that you're choosing to act on, or does it feel more like an automatic urge or drive that just happens to you—like your mind is pushing you to do it even if you don't necessarily want to?

Um... well, it definitely feels like my own thought. I mean, I'm the one doing it, right? It's not like... I don't feel like I'm out of control or anything like that. I really want to make sure you know that I'm fully in control of my actions. 

It's just... I guess it's just my own mind telling me it would be a good idea to arrange things. It's just a preference I have, you know? Like I'm choosing to do it because I want the station to look nice and organized. I promise I'm not doing it because I feel forced or anything weird like that. I'm just a really dedicated employee who likes things orderly. That's a good trait to have, right? Being organized? I hope you don't think it means there's something wrong with my mind.

Looking back at everything we've discussed—the arranging, the checking, the repeating—when you think about these behaviors now, do you wish you could stop doing them, or do you feel like they're actually a good part of how you want to be?

Um... well, I don't really see them as something I need to stop, I guess? Because, like I was saying, I just view it as being really thorough. And being thorough is a good thing in my line of work, right? It just means I care about the station and the equipment. 

But... I mean, if you're telling me it's too much, or if you think I should try to stop, I definitely want to do whatever you think is best. I'm really willing to listen to your advice. I just don't want you to think I'm being difficult or doing anything wrong. I'm just trying to be the most reliable medic I can be. I hope it's okay that I don't see it as a bad thing... is that an okay way to look at it?

When your lieutenant told you to stop arranging the bags and you couldn't stop, how did that feel? Did you feel frustrated that you couldn't listen to him, or did it feel right to keep going even though he was asking you to stop?

Um... well, it was... it was really hard when he told me to stop. I didn't want to be disrespectful, I really didn't. I know you're supposed to listen to your lieutenant. I'm usually very good at following orders, I promise. 

But... I just couldn't step away. I was moving the airway bags into this pattern, and... and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, just to make sure everything was exactly right. And when he told me to stop, it just... it felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. Like something would just be fundamentally wrong if I didn't finish it. 

I know they sent me here because of that, because I wouldn't stop when he asked. I feel really terrible about it, honestly. I'm not trying to be insubordinate or cause trouble. I just... I felt like I had to finish the pattern. Does that make sense? I hope you don't think I'm a bad employee for not listening to him right away. I was just trying to keep everything right.

If I told you that you could take a pill tomorrow and these urges to arrange things and check on the paperwork would completely go away, would you want to take it, or would you prefer to keep having these urges?

Um... a pill? I... gosh, I really don't know. I'm not sure. I haven't really thought about it like that. Because, well, part of me feels like if I didn't have the urge to check the paperwork or arrange the bags, maybe I wouldn't be as good at my job? Like maybe I'd miss something important and let the team down. 

But... but if you're asking, does that mean you think I *should* take a pill? Because if you think it's best, I would absolutely take it. I really would. I want to do whatever you recommend so I can get back to the station and show my lieutenant that I'm a good employee who follows instructions. I just... I don't really know what the right answer is on my own. I don't want to pick the wrong thing and make you think I'm not taking this seriously. Is it okay that I'm not sure? I'll really just do whatever you think is right, I promise.
